(CNN) -- A 13-year-old Minnesota boy who has cancer has resumed chemotherapy treatments and is not responding well, a family spokesman said Friday. Doctors say Daniel Hauser's lymphoma responded well to a first round of chemotherapy in February. Danny Hauser started a second round of chemotherapy treatment this week, Jim Navarro said in a statement on the family's Web site, dannyhauser.com. "The doctor changed the number of chemotherapy drugs in the protocol submitted to the court. Danny is not tolerating the drugs well and has been vomiting all day. He is understandably angry and depressed about being forced to go through the ravages of chemotherapy again." Daniel underwent his first round of chemotherapy in February, a month after he was diagnosed with Hodgkin's lymphoma. But his parents were concerned about the treatment's side effects, which typically include nausea, and decided to end the chemotherapy regimen and pursue holistic treatments instead. When Daniel's oncologist learned of the decision to reject standard treatment, which doctors say is associated with a cure rate of as high as 90 percent, he asked a court to intervene to ensure the teen got chemotherapy. Doctors say that, without it, the disease would likely prove fatal. But last week, before the court could act, Colleen Hauser packed up her son and flew with him to Southern California, from where they were planning to continue to Mexico to seek alternative alternative medical treatment. She said he would have run on his own had she not helped him flee. She changed her mind before crossing the border and returned this week with Daniel to Minnesota, where the family agreed to comply with whatever treatment the court ordered. A medical examination revealed that the boy's tumor had grown since he was diagnosed and the boy's doctor recommended he resume chemotherapy. After examining the boy on Monday, Dr. Michael Richards estimated the tumor's size at 5.3 inches by 5.1 inches by 6.3 inches, and said it was "protruding outside the chest wall." He said initiation this week of standard chemotherapy treatment was "imperative." Richards recommended at least another five cycles of chemotherapy followed by radiation, and added that the "goal will be to include alternative therapies in which the family is interested, as long as there is not data to suggest that a particular danger exists with any alternative medicine." District Court Judge John Rodenberg originally took custody of the boy away from his parents, but returned him to his family on the condition that they comply with the recommendations of the cancer specialist. Hodgkin's lymphoma is a cancer that affects the lymphatic system, which is part of the immune system. As the disease progresses, it compromises a body's ability to fight infection. CNN's Aaron Cooper contributed to this story.

# Family's Rejection of Chemotherapy Sparks Legal Battle Over Teen's Cancer Treatment

*A collision between parental rights, religious conviction, and medical authority raises difficult questions about who decides when a child's life hangs in the balance*

---

When 16-year-old Daniel Hartman was diagnosed with Hodgkin lymphoma last spring, his oncologist delivered news that, by most medical standards, should have been reassuring. The cancer was caught early. With a standard course of chemotherapy, Daniel's prognosis for a full recovery exceeded 85 percent—among the highest survival rates for any pediatric cancer.

But for the Hartman family, the recommended treatment represented not salvation, but a violation of deeply held beliefs about the body, healing, and faith. What followed was a months-long legal confrontation that pitted the family against the state, drew national attention, and reignited a long-running debate over the limits of parental authority.

## A Diagnosis and a Decision

The Hartmans, who live in a rural community roughly ninety minutes outside the state capital, describe themselves as devout believers in natural healing. For years, the family had avoided conventional medicine, relying instead on herbal remedies, nutritional therapies, and prayer.

"We don't reject the doctors because we don't love Daniel," his mother, Karen Hartman, said during an interview at the family's farmhouse. "We reject the poison because we do."

After the diagnosis, the Hartmans consulted a naturopathic practitioner two states away who offered an alternative regimen: an intensive protocol of vitamin therapy, dietary restriction, oxygen treatments, and supplements marketed as capable of shrinking tumors. The cost ran into the tens of thousands of dollars, none of it covered by insurance.

Dr. Ellen Ross, the pediatric oncologist originally assigned to Daniel's case, said she grew alarmed as weeks passed without treatment.

"I've spent my career watching this exact cancer respond beautifully to therapy," Ross said. "To watch a curable disease progress because of a decision made outside the exam room—it's the hardest thing a physician can face."

When Daniel missed a scheduled follow-up, and his parents informed the hospital they would not pursue chemotherapy, the medical team filed a report with child protective services.

## The State Intervenes

The case moved quickly into the family court system. State attorneys argued that Daniel, as a minor, was legally entitled to lifesaving medical care, and that his parents' refusal constituted medical neglect.

"The state does not lightly enter a family's home," said an attorney for the child welfare agency, who spoke on background. "But when the choice is between a proven cure and a preventable death, the government has both the authority and the obligation to act."

The Hartmans' attorney, Michael Devlin, framed the matter differently.

"This is a loving, intact family making a considered decision about their own child," Devlin argued before the court. "The question isn't whether the state prefers chemotherapy. The question is whether the Constitution allows the government to seize a child and force a medical procedure over the sincere objections of his parents."

At the center of the dispute stood Daniel himself—old enough to voice his own preferences, but not legally an adult. In a written statement to the court, Daniel said he did not want chemotherapy, citing both his faith and his fear of the treatment's side effects, which can include nausea, hair loss, and fatigue.

## The Question of the "Mature Minor"

The case turned in part on a legal concept known as the "mature minor doctrine," which some jurisdictions recognize as allowing older adolescents a degree of say in their medical care.

Legal scholars note that courts have historically been reluctant to defer entirely to minors on life-or-death questions.

"There's a meaningful difference between a 16-year-old refusing a treatment that might extend life by a few months in a terminal case, and refusing a treatment that offers a strong chance of a complete cure," said Professor Anita Coleman, who teaches health law. "Courts weigh the stakes. The higher the odds of survival, the more likely a judge is to order treatment."

Bioethicists have long grappled with the tension the case exposes. Dr. James Whitfield, a medical ethicist, described it as a conflict "between two values our society genuinely holds—the sanctity of family autonomy and the state's duty to protect vulnerable children."

"Reasonable people can feel the pull of both," Whitfield said. "That's what makes these cases agonizing."

## The Ruling

After several hearings, the court ruled in favor of the state. The judge ordered that Daniel receive chemotherapy under medical supervision, finding that the treatment's high success rate and the low risk to Daniel's long-term health outweighed the family's objections. Custody for medical decisions was temporarily assigned to a court-appointed guardian, though the Hartmans retained physical custody of their son.

In the written opinion, the judge acknowledged the sincerity of the family's beliefs but concluded that "the right to practice one's religion and to raise one's children according to one's conscience does not extend to a decision that would, by the weight of the medical evidence, cost a child his life."

The Hartmans initially indicated they would appeal, and for a period the case remained in legal limbo, drawing supporters on both sides who gathered outside the courthouse—some carrying signs defending parental rights, others advocating for Daniel's care.

## A National Conversation

The Hartman case is far from the first of its kind. Over the past two decades, similar disputes have unfolded across the country, several involving families who declined chemotherapy for children with treatable cancers. In some, courts ordered treatment; in others, families relocated or went into hiding to avoid intervention.

Advocacy groups on both sides have seized on these cases as emblematic of larger battles. Parental rights organizations warn of government overreach into the private sphere of the family. Child welfare advocates counter that a child's fundamental right to life cannot be subordinated to a parent's beliefs.

"The uncomfortable truth," said Coleman, "is that our legal system has no perfect answer. Every ruling in these cases satisfies one deeply held principle at the expense of another."

## An Uncertain Aftermath

As of this reporting, Daniel had begun the court-ordered treatment. Physicians involved in his care declined to discuss specifics, citing privacy, but sources familiar with the case said he was responding to therapy.

The Hartmans, for their part, remain unconvinced they were wrong. "We're doing what the court says because we have no choice," Karen Hartman said. "But I'll always believe there was another way."

For medical professionals, the case is a sobering reminder that even the most treatable diseases exist within a human context of belief, fear, and family.

"At the end of the day, I just want this young man to live," Dr. Ross said. "Everything else—the courts, the arguments, the headlines—none of it matters if we lose him. And none of it fully heals the wound this leaves behind, no matter how the story ends."
